item.title: Suppressing Implicit Output from PowerShell Methods and Expressions
item.description:
“Suppressing Implicit Output from PowerShell Methods and Expressions”

The Mechanism of Implicit Output in PowerShell

In PowerShell, unlike many programming languages relying solely on return values for data exchange, commands, expressions, and methods that generate output are automatically directed to the success output stream. This stream typically forwards data directly to the terminal unless specific actions are taken:

  1. Variable Assignment: Capturing the result, e.g., $variable = ....
  2. Pipeline Redirection: Sending the result down the pipeline, e.g., ... | Consumer.
  3. Stream Redirection: Explicitly sending the stream elsewhere, e.g., ... > $null.

Therefore, an operation like $range.BorderAround(1, -4138) functions similarly to Write-Output $range.BorderAround(1, -4138), necessitating explicit suppression if the return value is not intended for use.

Understanding the Challenge: Object Output vs. Value

By default, cmdlets like Select-Object create new objects, even when selecting a single property. When this object is piped to Add-Content, it’s the .ToString() representation of the entire object that gets written, not just the numerical value of the LoadPercentage. This can result in entries like @{LoadPercentage=4} in your log file, which is not ideal for simple numerical tracking.

item.title: PowerShell: Performance Impact of Array Increment Assignment
item.description:
“PowerShell: Performance Impact of Array Increment Assignment”

When constructing collections in PowerShell, particularly within loops, using the increment assignment operator (+=) can lead to significant performance degradation. This is due to how PowerShell handles arrays – they are immutable, meaning their size cannot change after creation. Every time += is used, PowerShell recreates the entire collection, appending the new item. This process becomes increasingly resource-intensive as the collection grows.

Why is += Inefficient?

The core of the inefficiency lies in this operation: $Collection = $Collection + $NewObject. For each iteration of a loop, PowerShell must allocate memory for a new array, copy all existing elements from the old array, and then add the new object. This repeated creation and copying is a major bottleneck.
